newsitem.title: CHINA: DENG'S BITTER BARGAIN: obey the party and prosper.
newsitem.headline: DENG'S BITTER BARGAIN: obey the party and prosper.

text.p: Three times citizens rose up to criticise China's authoritarian rule and three times Deng Xiaoping slapped them down, strong in his faith in the Communist Party's ultimate infallibility.

Though he himself pulled off modern China's crowning act of dissent -- defrocking his god-like predecessor, chairman Mao Zedong -- Deng lost little time after his 1978 ascent to power in setting the limits of post-Mao political debate.

"Our party has... made serious mistakes, but these were always corrected by the party itself, not by any other force," he said in 1980 after he strangled an early outpouring of dissent that became known as the Democracy Wall movement.
"No one is allowed to resist the leadership of the (party) Central Committee by using the Central Committee's mistakes as a pretext," Deng decreed.

Deng tolerated as useful the earliest "big-character posters" pasted on Democracy Wall, since they mainly attacked the same radical Maoist leftism that he himself was dismantling with a pragmatic embrace of market forces.

But after activist Wei Jingsheng appealed to citizens to seize power from the "hated old political system", Deng assailed this "so-called democrat" and imprisoned him for 15 years for espionage and sedition.
Democracy Wall was silenced.
In 1986, when tens of thousands of students took to the streets to demand that the party stop stage-managing elections and allow a real choice, Deng stood by his no-dissent decree.
He suppressed the protests and even sacked his top political protege, Hu Yaobang, the party chief he faulted for failing to recognise the threat of dissent.
But it was in June 1989 near Tiananmen Square that Deng displayed the cold brutality of his lifelong communist creed.

After weeks of watching Beijing citizens -- first students and later workers, intellectuals and even officials -- swarm into the streets to vent deep political frustration, Deng unleashed the army assault that bloodied his reformist epitaph.

Hundreds died and thousands were jailed as seditious counter-revolutionaries in the crackdown, which heralded years of repressive controls on dissent and purged another Deng heir, Zhao Ziyang, Hu's successor as party chief.
"There are so many Chinese people, and each has his own viewpoint," Deng told U.S. President George Bush in 1989.
"If there's a demonstration by this one today, and that one tomorrow, there'd be a demonstration every day, 365 days a year. In that case economic construction would be entirely out of the question."
Deng differed from Mao in handling dissent.
Deng struck an implicit bargain with China's people: support my reforms without argument, trust the party -- and you may get rich in the process.

As a result, Deng achieved what critics deemed impossible: year after year of dazzling double-digit economic growth despite stifling curbs on free speech, assembly, a free press and other political rights enshrined in China's constitution.

Chinese largely entered into the bargain out of a desire to prosper after two decades of suffering and want as well as a dread of the chaotic political swings that Mao actively abetted to further his own Machiavellian aims.

Mao had delighted in getting inside people's minds, testing their political loyalty, obliging them to "draw a clear line" between his revolution and China's traditions -- in effect forcing them to show their political stripe, sometimes with devastating or even deadly consequences.
In striking contrast, Deng tacitly allowed people a measure of privacy within their own thoughts and lives.

No longer were people arrested for listening to shortwave news from the Voice of America or the British Broadcasting Corporation. Gone were the humiliating "struggle sessions" in which Mao pitted Chinese against even their closest relatives.

Deng's 1978 "reform and opening up" created new problems, bringing an influx of foreign ideas, many of which clashed with party policy. He replied by attacking "spiritual pollution", "bourgeois liberalisation", "peaceful evolution" and other purported conspiracies that he saw as threatening to turn Chinese minds against communist rule.
The bargain largely held in the early 1980s, years when initial reforms brought small but satisfying gains and a palpable sense of progress after decades of suffering.

But its fragile logic began to unravel in the mid-1980s as those gains were threatened by twin scourges: inflation born of overheated economic growth and the corruption of officials and their families who enriched themselves at public expense.

The Tiananmen Square protests of 1989, unprecedented in size and popular appeal, were increasingly seen in subsequent years as having forced the party to take the people's anger seriously and attack their complaints aggressively.

Drives against corruption and inflation in the mid-1990s met with some success, partly validating Deng's belief in the Communist Party's ability to correct itself but also confirming the convinction of democrats that the Chinese people must rule the party, not the other way around.
